key_insight: Machine-learned long-time dynamics reveal that small polarons at reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move much more slowly than in the bulk because surface geometry removes most easy hopping pathways.
engineering_relevance: The results explain why porous rutile TiO2 can show lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, informing surface and defect engineering for catalysis, photovoltaics, and energy-storage devices.
method: Extended a machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics framework to an oxygen-deficient oxide surface.
Ran nanosecond-scale finite-temperature simulations on reduced rutile TiO2(110).
Analyzed polaron hopping pathways, layer-resolved motion, and vacancy effects on the free-energy landscape.
evidence_signal: The study used several nanoseconds of dynamics across multiple temperatures to quantify hopping statistics and found surface polaron mobility to be orders of magnitude lower than in bulk TiO2.
watch_item: The conclusions are specific to the modeled reduced rutile TiO2(110) surface and rely on the accuracy and transferability of the learned dynamics model.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
